title: A List of Debts
objective: Name three people and the specific thing each one taught you.

source.author: Marcus Aurelius
source.section: 1.1-1.3, and the closing line of Book 1
source.rights: Public domain in the United States
source.passage:
From my grandfather Verus I learned good morals and the government of my temper.

From the reputation and remembrance of my father, modesty and a manly character.

From my mother, piety and beneficence, and abstinence, not only from evil deeds, but even from evil thoughts; and further, simplicity in my way of living, far removed from the habits of the rich.

[...]

Among the Quadi at the Granua.

retrieval.answer: Acting the given part well is yours. Choosing the part belongs to another.

script.text:
Last week ended with a part to play. This week starts with the people who taught you how to play it.

Marcus Aurelius was a Roman emperor, and he kept a private notebook, written to himself rather than for readers. It opens in an unexpected place: not with a rule, but with a list of debts.

The first line reads: "From my grandfather Verus I learned good morals and the government of my temper." From his father's memory, modesty and a manly character. From his mother, piety and a habit of doing good, keeping clear of bad thoughts as well as bad deeds, and a simple way of living, far from the habits of the rich.

Notice how specific each line is. He doesn't thank his family in general. He names one person and what that person gave him.

After a week of asking what is within your power, it would be easy to picture a Stoic building a character alone. Marcus's notebook suggests otherwise. It opens by naming the people who shaped him.

In this translation, the first book closes with a note of where he was: Among the Quadi at the Granua. That was probably an army camp on the empire's frontier, far from Rome.

So here is today's page. Write three lines in his form: from this person, I learned this. Keep each one small and specific.

Tomorrow: how Marcus prepared for a day of difficult people.

outside_source_claims.claim: Marcus Aurelius was a Roman emperor (161-180 CE).
He wrote the Meditations as a private notebook, to himself rather than for readers.
The Granua note probably refers to an army camp on the empire's frontier.
outside_source_claims.note: Scholars aren't sure whether this line closes Book 1 or opens Book 2, which is why the script says in this translation.

check.scenario: A friend tells you they built their career entirely on their own, with no help from anyone.
check.question: Which response is closest to the way Marcus opens his notebook?

options.text: Agree. Real self-discipline means owing nobody anything.
options.feedback: Marcus was about as self-disciplined as anyone, and his book opens with a list of what he owed to other people.

options.text: Ask them who first showed them how to work that hard.
options.feedback: Marcus traces even his temper and his habits back to particular people. The effort was real, and someone usually showed you how.

options.text: Tell them gratitude is a nice feeling but not really philosophy.
options.feedback: Marcus's list isn't a feeling. It is a record: one person, one trait, written down so he can see where his character came from.

practice.text: Notice one person today doing something you would like to learn. Write it the way Marcus would: From ___, ___.
